questions.prompt: What is the intent of the Observer pattern?

options.text: Define a one-to-many dependency so that when a subject changes, all its observers are notified automatically
Encapsulate a request as an object
Capture and restore an object's state
Provide a simplified interface to a subsystem

questions.explanation: Observer is one-to-many automatic notification. Request-as-object = Command; capture/restore = Memento; simplify = Facade.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between push and pull delivery in Observer?

options.text: Push sends the changed data to observers; pull notifies minimally and observers fetch what they need
Push is always slower than pull
Pull sends all data; push sends none
They are the same

questions.explanation: Push hands observers the data; pull lets observers ask the subject for exactly what they want.

questions.prompt: What is the most common bug with Observer, and how do you avoid it?

options.text: A memory leak from observers that never unsubscribe — always remove an observer when it goes away
A stack overflow from cloning — always deep-copy
A race condition — always use two threads
A syntax error — always use interfaces

questions.explanation: Un-removed observers keep the subject referencing them, leaking memory and firing stray updates; unsubscribe when done.

questions.prompt: Is Observer the same thing as pub/sub or reactive programming?

options.text: No — it's the basis of them, but pub/sub adds a broker and reactive adds operators and scheduling
Yes, they are identical
Yes, but only in TypeScript
No — they are completely unrelated

questions.explanation: Observer is the core idea; pub/sub and reactive libraries build on it with extra machinery.

questions.prompt: Which are real consequences (good or bad) of Observer? Select all that apply.

options.text: Loose coupling between subject and observers
Observers can be added or removed at runtime
Memory leaks if observers aren't unsubscribed
A guaranteed notification order

questions.explanation: Observer gives loose coupling and runtime subscription but risks leaks; notification order is NOT guaranteed.

questions.prompt: Why did Java deprecate java.util.Observer/Observable in Java 9?

options.text: The naive built-in implementation was too limited — a caution about naive implementations, not the pattern itself
Because the Observer pattern is fundamentally broken
Because observers are always singletons
Because it converts interfaces incorrectly

questions.explanation: The pattern remains sound; Java's specific naive classes were deprecated in favor of better tools.
